summary.text: Each summand is decomposed as \(A_j\binom{n+j-1}{2j-1}+2A_j\binom{n+j-1}{2j}\), where \(A_j=(2j-1)^{\underline j}\); the coefficients \(A_j\) and \(2A_j\) are divisible by every positive integer up to their respective binomial lower indices, so Pascal’s identity implies invariance modulo the shift modulus when the upper index is shifted. Summing these termwise congruences gives the result, since the additional terms in the longer sum vanish through \(\binom nj=0\) for \(j>n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=n![x^n]\frac{e^x}{(1-x)^n}.
\]
We first put this into the finite-sum form used in the argument. For \(n\geq 1\), the expansions
\[
e^x=\sum_{i\geq0}\frac{x^i}{i!},\qquad
(1-x)^{-n}=\sum_{j\geq0}\binom{n+j-1}{j}x^j
\]
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=\sum_{i+j=n}\frac{n!}{i!}\binom{n+j-1}{j}\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^n \binom nj\binom{n+j-1}{j}j!.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, when \(i=n-j\), one has \(n!/i!=n!/(n-j)!=\binom njj!\). The same formula also holds for \(n=0\): both sides equal \(1\), with the sole summand interpreted as \(\binom00\binom00 0!=1\). Thus, throughout the proof, we may write
\[
a(n)=\sum_{r=0}^n P_r(n),\qquad
P_r(n):=\binom nr\binom{n+r-1}{r}r!.
\tag{1}
\]
As usual, \(\binom uv=0\) when \(v>u\). In the exceptional expression with \(n=r=0\), the second upper argument is understood as \(0\), as above.

We will prove that every individual function \(P_r(n)\) is periodic modulo an arbitrary modulus \(K\) under the shift \(n\mapsto n+K\). We then sum these congruences.

We use the falling factorial notation
\[
X^{\underline m}=X(X-1)\cdots(X-m+1),
\]
with value \(1\) for \(m=0\). When a lower factor would pass below zero, the corresponding natural-number falling factorial is zero. We repeatedly use
\[
X^{\underline m}=m!\binom Xm
\tag{2}
\]
and the splitting identity
\[
X^{\underline{A+B}}
 =X^{\underline A}(X-A)^{\underline B}.
\tag{3}
\]
Identity (3) follows simply by splitting the consecutive factors into the first \(A\) and the following \(B\) factors. We also use
\[
n(n-1)^{\underline m}=n^{\underline{m+1}}.
\tag{4}
\]
These identities remain valid in the zero cases because both relevant sides then vanish.

We next establish the main algebraic decomposition of a summand. For \(r\geq1\), put
\[
D_r=(2r-1)^{\underline r}=(2r-1)(2r-2)\cdots r.
\]
We claim that, for every \(n\geq0\),
\[
P_r(n)
 =D_r\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}
  +2D_r\binom{n+r-1}{2r}.
\tag{5}
\]

To prove this, first observe that
\[
(r!)^2\binom nr\binom{n+r-1}{r}
 =n(2r-1)!\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}.
\tag{6}
\]
By (2), the left side is
\[
n^{\underline r}(n+r-1)^{\underline r}.
\]
Using (4), then splitting the falling factorial by (3), this is
\[
\begin{aligned}
n(n-1)^{\underline{r-1}}(n+r-1)^{\underline r}
 &=n(n+r-1)^{\underline r}
       ((n+r-1)-r)^{\underline{r-1}}\\
 &=n(n+r-1)^{\underline{2r-1}},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the right side of (6) by (2).

We also need the adjacent-binomial relation
\[
n\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}
 =r\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}
  +2r\binom{n+r-1}{2r}.
\tag{7}
\]
If \(n\geq r\), the standard recurrence
\[
(m+1)\binom X{m+1}=(X-m)\binom Xm
\tag{8}
\]
with \(X=n+r-1\) and \(m=2r-1\) says
\[
2r\binom{n+r-1}{2r}=(n-r)\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1},
\]
and (7) follows after adding \(r\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}\). If \(n<r\), then \(n+r-1<2r-1\), so both binomial coefficients in (7) vanish, and (7) again holds.

Finally,
\[
r!D_r=r(2r-1)!.
\tag{9}
\]
Indeed, \(D_r(r-1)!=(2r-1)!\), since the two products supply exactly all factors from \(1\) through \(2r-1\), and \(r!=r(r-1)!\).

Multiply both sides of the proposed identity (5) by \(r!\). By (6), the resulting left side is
\[
n(2r-1)!\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}.
\]
Using (7), this equals
\[
(2r-1)!\left(
 r\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}
 +2r\binom{n+r-1}{2r}
\right).
\]
By (9), this is exactly \(r!\) times the right side of (5). Since \(r!>0\), cancellation proves (5).

We now prove a general binomial-shift lemma.

**Binomial-shift lemma.** Suppose \(m,C,X,K\) are nonnegative integers and every integer \(i\) with \(1\leq i\leq m\) divides \(C\). Then
\[
C\binom{X+K}{m}\equiv C\binom Xm\pmod K.
\tag{10}
\]

We prove this by induction on \(m\), with a subsidiary induction on \(X\). For \(m=0\), both sides equal \(C\). Suppose the result is known for \(m\), and consider order \(m+1\).

First take \(X=0\). The desired congruence is
\[
C\binom K{m+1}\equiv0\pmod K,
\]
because \(\binom0{m+1}=0\). If \(K=0\), this is simply equality, since \(\binom0{m+1}=0\). If \(K>0\), write \(C=(m+1)E\), which is possible by the divisibility hypothesis. Relation (8), with \(X=K-1\), gives
\[
(m+1)\binom K{m+1}=K\binom{K-1}{m}.
\]
Consequently
\[
C\binom K{m+1}=K E\binom{K-1}{m},
\]
which is divisible by \(K\).

Now suppose (10) at order \(m+1\) has already been proved for \(X\), and prove it for \(X+1\). Pascal's identity gives
\[
\binom{X+1+K}{m+1}
 =\binom{X+K}{m+1}+\binom{X+K}{m}
\]
and
\[
\binom{X+1}{m+1}
 =\binom X{m+1}+\binom Xm.
\]
After multiplication by \(C\), the first pair of terms are congruent by the subsidiary induction hypothesis at order \(m+1\). The second pair are congruent by the outer induction hypothesis at order \(m\); its divisibility assumptions hold because every \(1\leq i\leq m\) also lies between \(1\) and \(m+1\). Adding the two congruences proves (10). This completes both inductions.

We next check that the coefficients in (5) satisfy precisely the divisibility assumptions of this lemma.

For every \(r\geq1\),
\[
i\mid D_r\qquad(1\leq i\leq2r-1).
\tag{11}
\]
If \(i\leq r\), then \(i\mid r!\). Moreover, by (2),
\[
D_r=(2r-1)^{\underline r}=r!\binom{2r-1}{r},
\]
so \(r!\mid D_r\), and hence \(i\mid D_r\). If instead \(r<i\leq2r-1\), then \(i\) is literally one of the consecutive factors in
\(D_r=(2r-1)(2r-2)\cdots r\), so again \(i\mid D_r\). This proves (11).

Likewise,
\[
i\mid 2D_r\qquad(1\leq i\leq2r).
\tag{12}
\]
For \(i\leq2r-1\), this follows from (11). For the sole remaining value \(i=2r\), (11) with \(i=r\) gives \(r\mid D_r\), and therefore \(2r\mid2D_r\).

We can now prove termwise periodicity. Fix \(n,K\geq0\). For \(r\geq1\), apply the binomial-shift lemma first with
\[
m=2r-1,\quad C=D_r,\quad X=n+r-1,
\]
using (11), and then with
\[
m=2r,\quad C=2D_r,\quad X=n+r-1,
\]
using (12). We obtain
\[
D_r\binom{n+K+r-1}{2r-1}
 \equiv D_r\binom{n+r-1}{2r-1}\pmod K
\]
and
\[
2D_r\binom{n+K+r-1}{2r}
 \equiv2D_r\binom{n+r-1}{2r}\pmod K.
\]
Adding these congruences and invoking decomposition (5) on both sides yields
\[
P_r(n+K)\equiv P_r(n)\pmod K.
\tag{13}
\]
For \(r=0\), one has
\[
P_0(t)=\binom t0\binom{t-1}{0}0!=1
\]
(with the already noted natural convention at \(t=0\)), so (13) also holds for \(r=0\).

It remains only to pass from individual summands to \(a(n)\). Sum (13) over
\(0\leq r\leq n+K\). Congruences may be added, hence
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{n+K}P_r(n+K)
 \equiv
\sum_{r=0}^{n+K}P_r(n)
\pmod K.
\tag{14}
\]
The left side is \(a(n+K)\) by (1). On the right, every term with \(r>n\) is zero because it contains \(\binom nr=0\). Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{n+K}P_r(n)=\sum_{r=0}^nP_r(n)=a(n).
\]
Substitution into (14) gives
\[
\boxed{a(n+K)\equiv a(n)\pmod K}
\]
for all nonnegative integers \(n,K\). (When \(K=0\), the congruence means equality and is also immediate from \(n+K=n\).)
